profile.name: Line dance
profile.tagline: A choreographed group dance performed in rows without physical contact between dancers.
profile.insight: In 2014, Durham, North Carolina, was officially declared the line dancing capital of America based on the per capita density of local MeetUp groups.
profile.profile: Line dance is a choreographed form where individuals perform identical sequences of steps in parallel rows. Unlike partner dances, participants maintain no physical contact, allowing for a standardized, repeatable structure that can be adapted to diverse musical genres. Originating in its modern form during the 20th century, it has evolved from country-western roots into a global practice spanning pop, disco, and Latin styles.
profile.profile_long:
Line dance is a structured, choreographed form of movement where participants perform identical sequences of steps while arranged in parallel rows or lines. Unlike traditional partner dances, line dancers maintain no physical contact with one another, allowing the practice to be performed individually within a collective setting. The dance is defined by its repeatable nature; a specific sequence of steps is usually tied to a particular song, and these sequences are performed in cycles. Dancers typically face the same direction, though variations exist where lines face each other or change orientation throughout the dance. 

The development of modern line dance is primarily associated with the 20th century, drawing from a blend of folk traditions, show dance, and the influence of American television programs like 'American Bandstand'. While its roots are often linked to 19th-century European folk dances brought to North America, the 1970s disco era and the 1980s country-western boom were pivotal in establishing its current global popularity. The 1977 film 'Saturday Night Fever' and the 1992 hit 'Achy Breaky Heart' are frequently cited as catalysts that brought the form into the mainstream. 

Technically, line dances are categorized by the number of 'walls'—the directions a dancer faces at the end of a sequence. A one-wall dance returns the dancer to the starting orientation, while two-wall and four-wall dances involve turns of 180 or 90 degrees, respectively. Choreographies are often documented in 'step sheets' that detail the footwork, counts, and directional changes. While historically tied to country-western music, the genre has expanded to include pop, techno, Latin, and big band music, making it a versatile social activity practiced in clubs, ballrooms, and community centers worldwide.

sections.origins_and_history: Modern line dance emerged in the 20th century, with roots in European folk dances brought to North America in the 1800s. The 1957 'Madison' is considered one of the first true line dances. The 1970s disco era introduced dances like the 'L.A. Hustle' and 'Electric Slide', while the 1980s and 90s saw a surge in country-western line dancing, popularized by films like 'Urban Cowboy' and songs like 'Achy Breaky Heart'.
sections.how_it_is_danced: Dancers stand in rows, repeating a set sequence of steps. Movements are performed independently without physical contact. Choreographies are often based on counts of 32, 48, or 64, with syncopated steps like shuffles or chassés. Dancers may turn to face different 'walls' during the sequence.
sections.music_and_instruments: Originally tied to country-western music, line dance now incorporates pop, disco, Latin, rock, and techno. Instruments vary by genre, but the music must be suitable for a repeating, rhythmic step sequence.
sections.costume_and_setting: While historically associated with Western-style clothing and boots, modern participants often wear casual clothing and dance trainers. It is practiced in dance bars, social clubs, and ballrooms.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Line dance serves as a social activity and a form of recreational exercise. It is used in dance programs alongside other styles and is recognized as a competitive discipline in some regions.
sections.notable_figures: Ric L. Silver (choreographer of the Electric Slide), Max Perry, Jo Thompson Szymanski, Scott Blevins, and Bill Bader.
sections.regional_variants: Variations include contra-dance (lines facing each other), and regional styles influenced by local music scenes in the US, Europe, and Quebec.
sections.lineage: Evolved from 19th-century European folk dances and 20th-century show dance.

teaching.rhythm: Repeating sequences, often based on multiples of 8 counts.
teaching.formation: Parallel rows or lines, facing the same direction.
teaching.level_notes: Beginners start with 10-20 basic dances; advanced dancers may master over 100.

music_profile.sound_description: Music is chosen for its suitability to a repeating, rhythmic step sequence, spanning genres from country to pop and disco.

movement_profile.footwork: Repeating sequences of steps, shuffles, and turns.
movement_profile.formation_and_space: Parallel rows or lines; dancers face one or more 'walls'.

signature_moves.name: Turn
signature_moves.description: Rotation to face a new wall.

claims.text: Line dance is a choreographed dance in which a group of people dance along to a repeating sequence of steps while arranged in one or more lines or rows.
claims.quote: A line dance is a choreographed dance in which a group of people dance along to a repeating sequence of steps while arranged in one or more lines or rows.

claims.text: The Madison, created in 1957, is considered one of the first true line dances.
claims.quote: One of the first true line dances was the Madison, a novelty dance created and first performed in Columbus, Ohio, in 1957.

claims.text: The Electric Slide was choreographed by Ric Silver in 1976.
claims.quote: Einer der bekanntesten, noch heute getanzten Line Dances, der Electric Slide – auch als Freestyle bekannt, wurde 1976 von Ric Silver zu der Eröffnung der Discothek Vamps am Broadway in New York City choreografiert.

claims.text: Durham, North Carolina, was declared the line dancing capital of America in 2014.
claims.quote: Based on per capita ranking of MeetUp Groups in the US, Durham, N.C. was declared the line dancing capital of America in 2014.

claims.text: Line dances are categorized by the number of walls, which refers to the direction dancers face.
claims.quote: Line dances are commonly described by their number of walls. A wall is the direction in which the dancers face at any given time
